mainTopic: Openings for dissolving vows (the launderer story and the נולד question, threat-vows against a wife) and cancelling future vows in advance
overview: This amud finishes a story about a vow the חכמים struggled to dissolve. They sat so long that they moved from sun to shade and back. בטנית found the opening: would the man have vowed had he known the חכמים would suffer like this? He said no, and the vow was released. In a similar story, רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי kept rejecting every opening. Then a launderer hit him, and he said he would not have vowed had he known that would happen. רב אחא מדיפתי objects that being hit is a נולד, a new situation, and we may not open a vow with a נולד. רבינא answers that attacks on the חכמים by heretics were common, so it was not a נולד. Next, רב יוסף releases אביי's threat-vow against his wife, and a ברייתא shows that רבי יוסי did the same in a similar case. Finally, a new משנה teaches that one may cancel future pressure-vows in advance, and the גמרא asks how that plan could still pressure the friend.

steps.title: The Sages struggle for a long time to dissolve the vow
steps.stepSummary: The previous story ends with the חכמים unable to dissolve a man's vow. They are troubled and keep moving from sun to shade and back as the hours pass.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים were troubled, moving from the sun to the shade and from the shade to the sun.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes describing how long and hard the חכמים worked on someone's vow without finding a way to release it. This sets up the solution that comes soon.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To dissolve a vow, the חכמים need an opening: a fact the person did not expect when he made it. Here none was working, so the time dragged on. The detail about sun and shade shows that the sitting lasted long enough for the shadows to move.

phrases.english: And the Sages were troubled
from the sun to the shade and from the shade to the sun.
phrases.notes: As the day went on, the sun moved, so they kept changing seats. That shows how long they sat there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story from the end of the previous daf about a vow the חכמים could not release.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חכמים could not find an opening to dissolve the vow and spent a long, hard time trying.

steps.title: Another version: he kept saying yes to every opening
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tells the story a second way. The חכמים kept asking, 'Did you vow knowing this?' He answered 'yes' many times, and they stayed stuck from sun to shade and back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another version: 'Did you vow with this in mind?' 'Yes.' This happened many times, and the חכמים were troubled, moving from the sun to the shade and from the shade to the sun.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same story. It shows exactly why the חכמים were stuck: every opening they offered, he rejected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method for dissolving a vow is to ask, 'Did you vow knowing this would happen?' If he answers 'yes,' that opening fails. Here he kept saying 'yes,' so nothing worked, and the struggle dragged on.

keyTerms.meaning: with this in mind / knowing this

phrases.english: (Another version:
phrases.notes: Some versions have this whole bracketed section and some don't. It retells the same story in a second way.

phrases.english: "With this in mind?" "Yes."
phrases.notes: This is short for: the חכמים asked, 'Did you vow knowing this?' and he answered 'Yes.'

phrases.english: Many times,
and the Sages were troubled
from the sun to the shade and from the shade to the sun.)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Retells step 1 with more detail about why the חכמים were stuck.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every opening was rejected because the man said he had vowed knowing each fact.

steps.title: בטנית finds the opening: the חכמים' own trouble
steps.stepSummary: בטנית, son of אבא שאול בן בטנית, asks the man whether he would have vowed if he had known the חכמים would suffer like this. He says no, and they release the vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: בטנית, son of אבא שאול בן בטנית, said to him: 'Would you have vowed knowing that the חכמים would be troubled, moving from shade to sun and from sun to shade?' He said: 'No.' And they released it.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone finally finds a new fact the man never expected: the vow itself would cause the חכמים so much trouble. Because he would not have vowed knowing that, the vow is released.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The solution is clever. The opening is the very struggle that was going on. Once the man admits he never meant to cause the חכמים such distress, there is a real opening, and the vow can be dissolved.

keyTerms.meaning: בטנית, son of אבא שאול בן בטנית, the one who found the solution
would you have vowed? / did you vow?
they released it (they dissolved the vow)

steps.whatToRemember: An opening to dissolve a vow can come from the trouble the vow is causing right now to the חכמים, if the person admits he would not have vowed knowing it.

phrases.english: Botnit said to him,
the son of Abba Shaul ben Botnit:
"Would you have vowed knowing
that the Sages would be troubled
from the shade to the sun and from the sun to the shade?"
He said: "No." And they released it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the problem from steps 1-2 by turning the חכמים' distress into the opening.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new opening is found: the unexpected trouble caused to the חכמים.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the man said yes to every opening, it seemed the vow could not be released.
steps.terutzMaskana: He would not have vowed knowing the חכמים would suffer, so that became a valid opening, and the vow was released.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי keeps saying yes
steps.stepSummary: A second story: רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי wanted to dissolve a vow. To every opening the חכמים offered, he answered 'yes, I vowed with that in mind,' many times over.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי had a vow to dissolve. He came before the חכמים. They said: 'Did you vow with this in mind?' He said: 'Yes.' 'Did you vow with this in mind?' He said: 'Yes.' This happened many times.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a similar story about רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי. It sets up a scene where the חכמים again cannot find an opening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern matches the first story. Each opening the חכמים try is rejected, because he says he already knew that fact when he vowed. The scene is being set for an unexpected opening to appear.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei
had a vow to dissolve.
He came before the Sages,
they said to him: "Did you vow with this in mind?"
He said to them: "Yes."
"Did you vow with this in mind?"
He said to them: "Yes."
Many times.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בַּר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי הֲוָה לֵיהּ נִדְרָא לְמִישְׁרֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story with the same pattern as steps 1-3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי rejected every opening the חכמים offered.

steps.title: The launderer's blow becomes the opening
steps.stepSummary: A launderer saw the חכמים suffering and hit רבי ישמעאל with a launderer's tool. רבי ישמעאל said he would not have vowed had he known he would be hit, and the vow was released.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a certain launderer saw that the חכמים were troubled, he hit him with a launderer's tool. He said: 'I did not vow knowing that a launderer would hit me,' and he released the vow for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: A bystander gets angry and hits רבי ישמעאל. That blow creates a new, unexpected fact, which becomes the opening to release the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being hit by a launderer is something רבי ישמעאל clearly never imagined when he vowed. So he could honestly say he would not have vowed knowing it. That gave a real opening, and the vow was dissolved.

keyTerms.meaning: a launderer (one who cleans and beats cloth)
a launderer's tool (used to beat clothes)

steps.whatToRemember: Both stories teach the same idea: a vow can be released when the person admits he would not have vowed had he known some fact, and sometimes that opening comes from the struggle over the vow itself. The next step asks whether this launderer's blow was too new and unexpected to count.

phrases.english: When a certain launderer saw
that the Sages were troubled,
he hit him with a launderer's tool.
He said: "Knowing that a launderer would hit me
I did not vow,"
and he released it for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דַּחֲזָא הָהוּא קַצָּרָא דְּמִצְטַעֲרִי רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the standstill from step 4 with an unexpected event that creates an opening.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The launderer's blow served as the opening, and the vow of רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי was released through it. Steps 6-7 go on to examine whether this counts as a forbidden נולד.

steps.title: Isn't being hit by a launderer a new, unexpected situation?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדיפתי challenges the release of רבי ישמעאל's vow. Being hit by a launderer is a נולד, and a משנה says we may not open a vow with a נולד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא from דיפתי said to רבינא: This is a new situation, because no one would ever think a launderer would hit him. And we learned: we do not open a vow for a person using a new situation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the story we just finished. It says the release of רבי ישמעאל's vow seems to break a known rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To release a vow, you show the person he would not have vowed had he known some fact. But a נולד is something new that nobody could have expected when the vow was made, and such an opening is not allowed. Being hit by a launderer looks exactly like that, so how could they release the vow?

keyTerms.meaning: A new situation, something that came up after the vow and could not have been expected
'Opening': finding a reason that lets the vow be released

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
This is a new situation,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא מַסֵּיק אַדַּעְתָּא דְּמָחֵי לֵיהּ קַצָּרָא.
phrases.english: because it would not enter one's mind that the launderer would hit him.
And we learned: we do not open for him with a new situation!
phrases.notes: This is a rule from a משנה: you can't build the opening on something that only came up after the vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא הַאי נוֹלָד הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 5, where the vow was released because of the launderer's blow.
steps.kashyaTarget: The release of רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי's vow through the launderer's blow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being hit was totally unexpected, so it is a נולד, and the משנה forbids opening with a נולד.

steps.title: Attacks on the חכמים were common, so it is not something new
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that this is not a נולד. אפיקורסים often harassed the חכמים, so being attacked was something one could expect.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: This is not a new situation, because heretics who trouble the Rabbis are common.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends the release of the vow. Being attacked was not unthinkable, because heretics often bothered the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody could have predicted this particular launderer. But the general kind of event, someone hostile hurting a חכם, happened often enough to count as expected. So it is not a נולד, and the opening was valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Heretics who mock the Torah and its scholars

phrases.english: He said to him:
This is not a new situation,
since heretics who trouble the Rabbis are common.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הַאי לָאו נוֹלָד הוּא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the event falls under a common, expected kind of thing
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being hit by a launderer was totally unexpected, so it is a נולד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Attacks on the חכמים by heretics were common, so this was not a נולד and the release stands.
steps.whatToRemember: A נולד is something nobody could expect. If an event belongs to a common type of happening, it is not a נולד, even if the exact details were surprising.

steps.title: אביי's vow over whom the daughter would marry
steps.stepSummary: אביי and his wife disagreed about whom her daughter should marry. אביי vowed that she could not benefit from him if she married the girl to her own relative. She did it anyway, and רב יוסף released his vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי's wife had a daughter. He said she should marry his relative, and she said her relative. He told her: benefit from me will be forbidden to you if you go against my wishes and marry her to your relative. She went against him and married her to her relative. אביי came to רב יוסף, who asked him: if you had known she would go against you, would you have vowed? He said no, and רב יוסף released the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about releasing a vow. אביי's vow was meant as a threat, and when his wife ignored it, רב יוסף released it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי vowed only to pressure his wife, assuming she would give in. רב יוסף's opening was: had you known she would defy you anyway, would you have vowed? Since the answer was no, the vow was released.

keyTerms.meaning: Benefit from me is forbidden to you

phrases.aramaic: דְּבֵיתְהוּ דְּאַבָּיֵי הֲוָה לַהּ הָהִיא בְּרַתָּא.
phrases.english: Abaye's wife had a certain daughter.
He said: to my relative.
She said: to her relative.
He said to her: benefit from me should be forbidden to you

phrases.aramaic: אִי עָבְרַתְּ אַדַּעְתַּאי וּמַינְסְּבַת לַהּ לְקָרִיבָךְ.
phrases.english: if you go against my wishes and marry her to your relative.
She went and went against his wishes
and she married her to her relative.
He came before Rav Yosef.
He said to him: if you had known

phrases.aramaic: דַּעֲבַרַת עַל דַּעְתָּךְ וּמַנְסְבָא לַהּ לְקָרִיבַהּ
phrases.english: that she would go against your wishes and marry her to her relative,
would you have made the vow?
He said: No. And Rav Yosef released it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵיתְהוּ דְּאַבָּיֵי הֲוָה לַהּ הָהִיא בְּרַתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about releasing a vow, after the launderer discussion ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow made as a threat can be released by asking: had you known she would defy you anyway, would you have vowed?

steps.title: Can a vow really be released this way?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a vow may be released with this kind of opening, which is based on the very thing the vow was about.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is a vow released in a case like this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב יוסף's ruling. It is setting up the next step, which brings a source to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opening uses the exact event the vow was conditioned on, her defying him. One might think that event was obviously in his mind when he vowed, so it should not count as a reason to release. The גמרא asks whether such a release really works.

phrases.english: And is it released in a case like this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions whether רב יוסף's release in step 8 was valid.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a vow can be released by asking 'had you known she would defy you, would you have vowed?'

steps.title: Yes: רבי יוסי did the same with a vow about going up for the festival
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes and brings a ברייתא. A man vowed against his wife going up for the רגל. She went anyway, and רבי יוסי released the vow with the same kind of question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, and it is taught: A man vowed against his wife going up for the festival. She went against his wishes and went up. He came to רבי יוסי, who asked: had you known she would defy you and go up, would you have vowed at all? He said no, and רבי יוסי released it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question with a ברייתא that matches the אביי story almost exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both stories a husband vowed to stop his wife from doing something, and she did it anyway. רבי יוסי used the same opening as רב יוסף, so רב יוסף's ruling has an earlier source.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it is taught', bringing a ברייתא as support
Made a vow forbidding someone something
To go up to ירושלים for the festival

phrases.english: Yes, and it is taught:
There was an incident with one man
who vowed against his wife going up for the festival,
and she went against his wishes and went up for the festival,
and he came before Rabbi Yosei.
He said to him: and if you had known
that she would go against your wishes and go up for the festival,
would you have vowed against her at all?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: לֹא, וְהִתִּירוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
phrases.english: He said to him: No, and Rabbi Yosei released it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 with a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes, such a vow may be released, as רבי יוסי did in the same kind of case.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about רבי יוסי releasing a husband's vow about going up for the רגל
steps.whatToRemember: When a husband vows only to stop his wife from doing something, and she does it anyway, the vow can be released by asking: had you known she would do it anyway, would you have vowed?

steps.title: Cancelling your future vows ahead of time
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב teaches that someone who plans to make a vow only to pressure his friend to eat with him can declare in advance that his future vows are void, as long as he remembers this when he vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: Even one who wants to vow against his friend so that he will eat with him should say: 'Any vow I make in the future is void,' as long as he remembers this at the time of the vow.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches a way to make future vows not count by declaring ahead of time that they are void.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes a person vows only to push a friend to eat with him, without wanting a real vow. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says he can cancel such vows in advance by saying any vow he makes will be void. This only works if he remembers that declaration when he makes the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: To make a vow that pressures his friend
At the time of the vow

steps.confusionAlert: He is not releasing a vow after the fact. He is setting things up beforehand so the vow never takes effect at all.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
Even one who wants to vow against his friend
phrases.notes: The word 'even' links back to the earlier משנה about vows that were never meant seriously.

phrases.english: so that he will eat with him,
should say to him:

phrases.aramaic: ״כׇּל נֶדֶר שֶׁאֲנִי עָתִיד לִידּוֹר הוּא בָּטֵל״,
phrases.english: "Any vow that I will make in the future is void,"
provided that he remembers at the time of the vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר אַף הָרוֹצֶה לְהַדִּיר אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, moving from releasing vows after the fact to cancelling them in advance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person can declare ahead of time that his future vows are void, as long as he remembers this declaration when he makes the vow.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה is the source the גמרא will use to discuss cancelling future vows in advance.

steps.title: If the vow is already cancelled, why would the friend listen?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's advice. If the host already declared that all his future vows are void, his friend will know the vow means nothing and will not come to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Since he already said, 'Every vow I will make in the future should be void,' his friend will not listen to him and will not come with him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה with a challenge. It asks how the plan can work if the host's own announcement makes his pressure-vow empty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole point of the host's vow is to push his friend into coming. But once the host has said in advance that his vows are void, the friend knows the vow has no force and will ignore it. The plan seems to defeat itself, so the גמרא needs to explain how it could work.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion of the משנה begins here

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the advance cancellation fails legally. It is asking a practical question: how can the host still pressure his friend if the friend knows the vow is void?

phrases.english: GEMARA:
And since he said:
phrases.notes: "He" is the host from the משנה in step 11, the one who wants his friend to come eat with him.

phrases.aramaic: ״כׇּל נֶדֶר שֶׁאֲנִי עָתִיד לִידּוֹר יְהֵא בָּטֵל״,
phrases.english: 'Any vow that I will vow in the future should be void,'
he (the friend) will not listen to him
and will not come with him!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דְּאָמַר כׇּל נֶדֶר שֶׁאֲנִי עָתִיד לִידּוֹר יְהֵא בָּטֵל לָא שָׁמַע לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה quoted in step 11 by challenging whether its advice makes practical sense.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's advice to declare future pressure-vows void in advance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A vow meant to pressure the friend works only if the friend thinks it is binding. A declaration that makes the vow void would remove that pressure, so the plan seems to defeat itself.
